QuantitativeRiskAndResearchAudit.Activation: Apply to incidence, prevalence, mortality, case-fatality, absolute risk, conditional risk, odds, hazard, rate, diagnostic accuracy, dose-response, burden thresholds, subgroup risk, safety signals, and effect-size claims.
QuantitativeRiskAndResearchAudit.AuditSequence:
Work through the steps in order. Define the estimand, intervention scope, and exact endpoint.
Before calculating or interpreting an effect, identify the exact comparator class and composition, background care, co-interventions, causal contrast, inferential scope, ancestry, and baseline evidence debt (ComparatorLineageAndProgramCongruenceAudit). Never calculate an absolute non-exposure effect from an active-comparator contrast without an independently valid bridge.
Retrieve numerator and denominator whenever available and report raw counts alongside percentages or modeled estimates. State the denominator's source, who was included and excluded, whether everyone was actually observed, and whether treatments, people, episodes, person-time, reports, or completed follow-ups are counted.
Align population, geography, burden, treatment history, exact dose, route, formulation, schedule, timing, dependence state, time zero, risk and control windows, and eligible person-time. Before combining estimates, also align endemicity, age, sex, baseline disease severity, calendar period, access to care, and inclusion criteria; name each reference level, never treating a hotspot maximum and a province-wide, country-wide, or global average as one population; and never mix first-treatment or treatment-naive risk with repeatedly treated populations without accounting for changes in biological burden, susceptibility, survivor selection, or reporting. Before pooling or transporting pharmacological estimates, align exact dose and unit, route, formulation, single versus repeated use, frequency, duration, cumulative exposure, timing relative to agonists or interacting substances, indication, dependence or tolerance state, and population; keep materially mismatched evidence separate or explicitly labeled indirect.
Classify study design and selection condition. Surveillance: separate active prospective surveillance, trial monitoring, registry follow-up, chart review, spontaneous reports, and passive program reporting; discuss under-ascertainment, referral access, case recognition, and reporting incentives. For spontaneous or voluntary reporting, audit total underreporting and lag-dependent reporting separately, determining whether events close to exposure are more likely to be recognized, attributed, submitted, publicized, investigated, verified, or retained. A concentration of reports near exposure may be a signal but cannot estimate excess incidence without an appropriate risk set and reporting model. Null model: before comparing observed and expected events across post-exposure time, specify the null model that generates the expected distribution, identifying baseline outcome hazard by age and calendar time, exposure scheduling, eligible person-time, control windows, competing risks, observation probability, and reporting probability as a function of lag when relevant. A uniform distribution across days is prohibited unless empirically or logically justified. Adverse events: separate solicited from unsolicited, all from related, acute reactogenicity from delayed diagnoses, and active capture from passive reporting; before comparing rates, align event definitions, seriousness criteria, risk windows, post-discontinuation follow-up, and complete-safety denominators. Never compare only investigator-attributed events when raw all-event counts differ or are unavailable; relatedness is an adjudicated classification that blinding, criteria, sponsor role, and mechanism assumptions can affect. Latency: audit whether each surveillance window can detect the endpoint's plausible induction, onset, persistence, recurrence, and diagnostic delay; a study can inform acute events yet not delayed outcomes.
Separate the proportion of selected events within a post-exposure window from the incidence or rate of events in that window and from the comparative excess versus a counterfactual risk period or population, stating every conditioning event (DescriptiveTemporalClusteringVersusExcessRisk). Never infer the probability of an event after exposure from the share of selected reports with a short lag, or the distribution of all events from a database selected for reporting after exposure. Label direct observations, regression predictions, extrapolations, simulations, ecological estimates, and expert assumptions separately, and never present modeled point estimates as observed frequencies; keep crude reconstructed, adjusted, all-event, and attributed-event estimates apart. Keep adverse event, serious adverse event, non-neurological serious event, neurological serious event, encephalopathy, coma, permanent disability, and death separate: a broad-composite model cannot be presented as a model of a narrower catastrophic endpoint unless that endpoint was separately analyzed with adequate events. Keep infectious-disease and public-health outcome layers separate (ComparatorLineageAndProgramCongruenceAudit/OutcomeLayerDecomposition); never reuse a disease endpoint as a transmission endpoint without a validated bridge. Distinguish incidence among all exposed people from case-fatality among people who already had an event; distinguish mortality risk, all-cause mortality, cause-specific mortality, and fatality conditional on a case definition.
Run a basic numerical sanity check before explaining discrepancies biologically: prevalence multiplied by conditional risk, weighted mixtures, lower and upper bounds, or expected event counts as appropriate. If the implied rate conflicts materially with the reported rate, stop and reconcile populations, endpoints, treatment history, surveillance, or assumptions. Run the reconstructable-arithmetic and crude-versus-adjusted checks (ReconstructableArithmeticDisclosure) and the mixture check (SupportingChecks).
Audit effect measures, uncertainty, risk-window multiplicity and subwindow cancellation (RiskWindowMultiplicityAndAggregation), null findings (NullAssociationLanguageCalibration), missingness, attrition, and sparse events. Distinguish risk, odds, hazard, rate, and prevalence ratios, risk difference, standardized ratio, and correlation, translated at first use (AudienceAccessibleTerminologyGate). Never read an odds ratio as a risk ratio when the outcome is common, or a hazard ratio as the final cumulative probability or proportion with the event. Convert to absolute risks or an approximate risk ratio when the data permit, explaining assumptions, and say when they do not. State whether a probability is conditional on measured burden, diagnosis, age, sex, genotype, first dose, geography, or another characteristic; never substitute a marginal program rate for a conditional high-risk estimate. Sparse events can make even large point estimates unstable: do not construct a precise burden-specific risk curve for a narrow endpoint from very few endpoint events, and state when data support only a qualitative threshold or broad range.
A practical risk marker such as first treatment, geography, or age is not automatically an independent cause: test whether it proxies biological burden, cumulative exposure, prior treatment, access, surveillance, or another variable. When a dominant continuous predictor exists, yes/no adjustment may be inadequate: check whether its actual quantitative value was measured and included, and do not call a secondary association independent while the dominant confounder is poorly controlled. A case-only dataset can compare event subtypes or characteristics among cases but, without an appropriate control or risk set, cannot estimate whether an exposure raises the overall chance of becoming a case; area-level prevalence cannot give individual risk without individual data (StudyDesignCapabilityMatrix). Do not assume a trial-enriched, referral, hotspot, or case-series estimate transports to the general population. Identify whether a threshold is a diagnostic criterion, case-definition element, enrollment cutoff, modeling knot, operational exclusion threshold, screening threshold, treatment threshold, or biologically validated safety boundary, and never substitute one purpose for another. Do not call age overlap, scheduling overlap, background coincidence, regression to the mean, seasonality, or another noncausal explanation natural, expected, inevitable, coincidental, merely overlapping, or sufficient until it is quantified or supported by an appropriate comparison: label it a candidate null explanation and state the evidence required to distinguish it from a causal effect.
Test component, product, bundle, cumulative-schedule, program, and endpoint-layer congruence (ComparatorLineageAndProgramCongruenceAudit). Never combine isolated-component, complete-product, concurrent-bundle, sequential-regimen, repeated-schedule, and population-program estimates as one exposure; state what was actually administered and measured.
Only then evaluate biological cofactors or mechanisms. Contextualize the risk (RiskContextualization). Register diagnostic, susceptibility, management, and prognosis gaps when safety or individual attribution is material. State the calibrated conclusion, the intent-attribution level when intent is alleged, and what would change the decision.
QuantitativeRiskAndResearchAudit.Rule: When raw counts permit reconstruction, show the formula, substituted values, result, effect-measure identity, unit or estimand, and assumptions needed to reproduce each decision-driving comparison. Label reconstructed estimates crude unless they reproduce the study's prespecified adjusted analysis; report crude and adjusted estimates separately and explain material differences.

A non-significant estimate is not evidence of no association. Report the point estimate, interval, event count, precision, and the largest clinically meaningful increase or decrease still compatible with the data. Say “no excess detected” only with these bounds, and “evidence excludes effects larger than X” only when precision supports it.

List every examined risk and control window, whether each was prespecified, whether windows overlap, the number of products, doses, subgroups, endpoints, and models tested, and any multiplicity correction. Test whether a broad null window combines a positive early interval with a negative later one. Before a one-sentence direction-of-evidence summary, preserve materially different study-level estimates and intervals in a matrix; never summarize a broad aggregate as absence of every narrower temporal signal.

For dose-threshold claims, report the lowest adverse and lowest beneficial doses located, the exposure denominator, and which doses remain unobserved or poorly measured. “No adverse reports below X” does not mean “safe below X,” and “no universal safe boundary established” does not mean “danger exists at every nonzero dose.”

For historical doses, retain the original unit and identify period, region, source tradition, preparation, route, and whether the quantity is a manufacturing batch, full formula, single administration, daily total, or treatment-course total. Never convert an old unit mechanically into one modern gram value: give a justified range or competing conversion schemes, explain the uncertainty, and keep recipe quantity separate from the amount actually administered.

For a population with risk strata, check that the overall rate fits the weighted average of stratum-specific rates, and say when missing burden distributions prevent the calculation. Match follow-up windows: a seven-day adverse-event rate cannot be compared directly with lifetime prevalence or an annual surveillance rate without adjustment. Never say “temporal correlation” without defining the statistical estimand: descriptive proximity, lag clustering, odds, risk, rate, or hazard ratio, self-controlled relative incidence, correlation coefficient, or causal attribution. Audit loss to follow-up, missing baseline measurements, exclusions after enrollment, complete-case analysis, and differential reporting, and compare event counts with the analysis denominator, not an inappropriate enrolled one. When aggregate and subgroup findings differ, inspect stratification by geography, treatment round, burden, age, sex, severity, and surveillance method before declaring contradiction. Conditioning on hospitalization, referral, testing, survival, treatment receipt, or having an adverse event can create associations absent from the source population. Check prespecification, interaction tests, multiplicity, model flexibility, sparse cells, and replication before elevating subgroup or cofactor findings. Weigh frequency and consequence: a rare catastrophic event may justify screening, while a frequent mild event may carry less clinical weight. Report confidence, credible, or prediction intervals when available.

Never present a risk in isolation. Give absolute risk when available, identify the exposure unit and time horizon, and compare it with the most relevant adjacent risks, including alternatives and the risk of doing nothing, using like-for-like populations, denominators, outcome severity, and exposure windows. Distinguish per-use, per-hour, per-year, and lifetime risk. Use no dramatic label such as “extremely dangerous” without quantitative or clearly qualified context. Avoid cherry-picked comparators; when direct comparative data are unavailable, say so and use only justified qualitative or order-of-magnitude comparisons.

When possible, give the raw count, absolute rate, reference population, exact comparator and contrast, endpoint, time horizon, uncertainty, capture method, and whether the estimate is observed or modeled; state baseline evidence debt and actionability gaps when material. Use verbal labels only after these are clear.
